title: Sleep softly
hook: an unnamed nun is told: sleep softly in the robe you made, your passion stilled like herbs dried in a pot (Therigatha 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. Your line was her own words. Which line did you carry from your poem? Today, the first poem in the book. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

A robe, sewn by the woman who will wear it. A pot on a shelf where herbs have dried out. And a voice saying: sleep softly. That's nearly the whole of the first poem in the Therigatha. It's only a few lines long, and the nun it speaks to has no name. The heading calls her a certain elder nun, and that's all. The book of the nuns' own words opens not with a queen or a famous teacher, but with a woman nobody wrote down by name. Today, the opening poem.
screen: `A ROBE SHE SEWED.` → `HERBS DRIED IN A POT.` → `A NUN WITH NO NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the nun with no name. Some readers find a quiet welcome in that: the first words of the collection go to someone whose name wasn't kept. She could be anyone who sat in a robe and practiced. Second, the robe. In the poem she is told to sleep softly, wrapped in the robe she made herself. Her rest isn't borrowed. She's resting inside her own work, a robe she made for herself. Third, the herbs. The reason she can sleep, the voice says, is that her passion is stilled, like herbs dried in a pot. Green leaves are full of sap. Leave them in a pot and the moisture goes out of them. They don't fight. They just dry. The craving that used to pull at her has lost its sap in the same way. There's nothing left in it to sprout. Fourth, what the poem asks of her. Not to strive harder. Not to teach anyone. Not to prove anything. It says sleep. Freedom, in this first poem, is pictured as rest after long work. In Pali the phrase is sukham supahi, sleep at ease, and sukha is the ordinary word for ease and happiness, the word that stands across from dukkha, suffering. So the book of the nuns begins with permission. A woman is told she can lie down, wrapped in what she made, and sleep without anything tugging at her.
screen: `A NUN WITH NO NAME.` · `A ROBE SHE MADE HERSELF.` · `LIKE HERBS DRIED IN A POT.` · `REST AFTER LONG WORK.` · then, large: `SLEEP SOFTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in something you made. Settle, and let the breath lengthen on its own. Find one thing nearby that your own hands made or shaped: a meal, a made bed, a folded sweater, a cleaned counter, a page you wrote. If nothing is within reach, choose one from memory. Let your attention rest on it, the way she rested in her robe. Nothing to improve. Nothing to add. Just rest in something finished. The bell holds the time.
Sleep softly. The first poem of the Therigatha: a nun with no name, told to rest in the robe she made, her passion stilled like herbs dried in a pot. Today's word.
Your line: sleep softly. Tonight, before sleep, lay a hand on one thing you made today, and let the day be finished. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of the Therigatha meet this short poem first, and teachers in some Buddhist communities use it to speak about rest and contentment as part of the path, not a break from it.

fork.reveal: the first poem of the nuns' book is permission to rest: sleep softly, wrapped in your own work.

original.note: Pali sukhaṃ supāhi: sleep at ease, sleep softly. The opening words of the poem.

trapdoor: what it means: a nun whose passion has dried out like herbs in a pot is told she can rest, wrapped in the robe she made.
what a scholar hears: the Pali opens sukham supahi, sleep at ease; sukha is the everyday word for ease and happiness, the opposite of dukkha.

notes: Thig 1.1 paraphrased: 'sleep softly/at ease, little elder nun, wrapped in the robe you made yourself; your passion is stilled like herbs dried in a pot'. Confirm the image (herbs/vegetables withered in a pot) and that the robe is one she made herself.
The heading 'a certain elder nun' (aññatarā therī): confirm.
The commentary says the verse was spoken to her by the Buddha; the script says only 'a voice'. Confirm whether to name the speaker.
Original: सुखं सुपाहि (sukhaṃ supāhi) as the poem's opening words; confirm the Pali and Devanagari.
'Some readers find a quiet welcome' in the nun being unnamed is attributed reading, not a text claim.
Audit: cut 'the cloth she cut and stitched with her own hands' (detail beyond the verse; some translators render the robe as made from rags, cholehi). Keeper may prefer to mention the rag robe.
